name: Crispy Ambulance
label: Factory Records
lede: Four South Manchester teenagers who started out covering Hawkwind ended up with Rob Gretton in their corner, Martin Hannett at the desk, and their singer fronting Joy Division for one chaotic night in Bury.

eras.title: Hawkwind covers to the Factory club
eras.text: Alan Hempsall and Robert Davenport began as a duo playing Magazine and Hawkwind songs. Within eighteen months they were a four-piece playing Band on the Wall and the Cyprus Tavern, and Joy Division had noticed.

years.cap: Crispy Ambulance's first gig, Spurley Hey Youth Club, Manchester, 1978
years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: First gig, New Year's Day, at Spurley Hey Youth Centre
years.p: [[Alan Hempsall|573ece44-8d4d-4a90-aaed-90ead4adb8f0]] and [[Robert Davenport|bc60a85f-f254-4b03-b32d-54c6efe6bd9f]] played as a duo, then brought in Keith Darbyshire on bass and Gary Madeley on drums.
years.xp:
Hempsall on the Hawkwind covers: "Hawkwind were like the step-brothers of punk. Very anarchic, and all their songs were just as easy to play."

The name came from [[Graham Massey|6739352a-3f16-418b-ba43-6c41912badc5]], later of [[Biting Tongues|555ac13e-6428-4a1a-8284-5c18d4e29330]] and [[808 State|36f35db0-bc09-43e7-8650-a123224943c7]], per LTM.

years.cap: Crispy Ambulance at the Factory Night, Russell Club, Hulme, 13 July 1979
years.src: LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Joy Division spot them, and Gretton puts them on at the Factory
years.p: After seeing Crispy Ambulance in 1978, [[Joy Division|9a58fda3-f4ed-4080-a3a5-f457aac9fcdd]] introduced them to manager [[Rob Gretton|41b55fab-da3b-4ecf-a67d-aeeec338a9c5]]. Next July the band shared a Factory club night in Hulme with Joy Division.

eras.title: The year everything turned on Joy Division
eras.text: Crispy Ambulance put out a do-it-yourself single, its singer stood in for Ian Curtis in Bury, and after Curtis's death the band's champion became a Factory director.

years.cap: Crispy Ambulance at Elizabeth Gaskell College, Manchester, March 1980
years.src: Wikipedia: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Hempsall sings for Joy Division at Derby Hall, Bury, and it ends in a riot
years.p: Ian Curtis had attempted suicide the day before, per Wikipedia. Hempsall stood in for three songs; the night descended into a riot and later turned up in the film Control.
years.xp: Wikipedia cites Deborah Curtis's Touching from a Distance for the account. The scene was restaged in Anton Corbijn's 2007 film Control.

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
yt: From the Cradle to the Grave
years.h: From the Cradle to the Grave on their own Aural Assault label
years.p: The debut single, backed with Four Minutes From the Frontline, was pressed in 1,000 copies, then 4,000.
years.xp:
Hempsall: "We'd tried Rough Trade and Factory and they'd turned us down. Rob Gretton encouraged us to do a do-it-yourself single."

Demos had been cut at Graveyard Studio in Prestwich.

years.big: Worst band name on Factory, said Tony Wilson
q: Tony never liked us, but suffered us because Rob liked what we did.
years.src: Wikipedia: Unsightly and Serene · Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Gretton becomes a Factory director and signs Crispy Ambulance
years.p: After Ian Curtis's death in May, Gretton joined Factory as a director and brought the band onto the label. [[Tony Wilson|124a6f5d-b2e0-4a75-95ad-db4c38063e02]] went along with it.
years.xp:
Hempsall says Wilson had no choice once Gretton was an equal shareholder. Per Factory Benelux, Wilson later called Crispy Ambulance the worst band name on Factory.

That same summer Hempsall turned down an invitation to audition as singer for the band that became [[New Order|f1106b17-dcbb-45f6-b938-199ccfab50cc]], and Crispy Ambulance cut a session for Piccadilly Radio.

years.src: Wikipedia: Unsightly and Serene · LTM: Crispy Ambulance · Wikipedia: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Factory issues Unsightly and Serene on 10-inch
years.p: FAC 32, produced by Stewart Pickering and recorded in June, with Not What I Expected on the B-side.
years.xp: A John Peel session followed in January 1981. Those tracks and the Piccadilly session later filled out LTM's archive CD Frozen Blood (2000).

eras.title: Thirteen minutes with Hannett, eight days with Nagle
eras.text: Martin Hannett's single and the album that followed are the band's core records. Critics were rough on The Plateau Phase at the time; it has been reappraised since.

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: [[Martin Hannett|ffbfce58-5185-4bcc-8c45-a7cd5d1a3783]] produces Live on a Hot August Night
years.p: Cut at Cargo Studio, Rochdale, in January, with The Presence running over 13 minutes and Concorde Square on the other side. Its oddness moved the band to Factory Benelux.
years.xp:
Hempsall says Hannett "just sat at the back and did very little at all, and let John Brierley do all the engineering", and didn't want the band around for the mix at Britannia Row. Hannett's one big intervention, an ARP 2600 on the vocal outro, split opinion.

Decades later Poet Laureate Simon Armitage picked The Presence as his inheritance track on BBC Radio 4.
play: Live on a Hot August Night

years.cap: Crispy Ambulance in A Breath of Fresh Air zine, Preston, 1982
years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Across Holland with [[Section 25|82e26f64-813d-4b22-a442-44d182f7f9eb]], plus Bochum and Brussels
years.p: Wally van Middendorp of [[Minny Pops|68142098-e3b3-4f76-a8cc-8898713fcf58]] set up six Dutch dates and two more. Soundman Jon Hurst taped the shows, and Sexus was recorded in Brussels between gigs.

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance · Wikipedia: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: The Plateau Phase, FBN 12, in a lilac sleeve
years.p: Lucien De Roeck designed the sleeve and the album made the indie chart top 25. NME called it "pretentious, turgid and tedious".
years.xp:
Chris Nagle replaced Hannett and the album was cut in eight days at Strawberry 2 in September 1981. Hempsall: "Chris allowed us to experiment freely."

Sounds writer Dave McCullough stood by it. Bob Stanley later called closing track Simon's Ghost "a beautifully eerie thing".

years.src: LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Last gig at the Adub Club, Nottingham, all new songs
years.p: The four kept going as Ram Ram Kino, with a bigger lineup.

eras.title: Ram Ram Kino
eras.text: The Brussels single surfaced two years late while the same four people chased a new name.

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · Wikipedia: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Sexus, recorded on tour in 1982, arrives on Factory Benelux
years.p: Up-tempo, cut quickly at Little Big One in Brussels, backed with Black Death (Life Is Knife).

years.src: LTM: Crispy Ambulance · Wikipedia: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: As Ram Ram Kino, one single on Psychic TV's Temple label
years.p: EMI paid for demos, but Advantage (Tantric Routines 1-4) was the only release. LTM says the name is German slang for a porn cinema; the project folded in 1987.

eras.title: Back at Band on the Wall
eras.text: All four originals reunited in 1999 and made two new albums with Graham Massey producing, the man who'd named them.

years.cap: Flyer for the reunion at Toolshed, Band on the Wall, 5 November 1999
years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: The original four reunite at Band on the Wall
years.p: A one-off after weeks of rehearsal, released as the live CD Accessory After the Fact, mixed by Massey.

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Scissorgun on Darla, and four US dates
years.p: The first new album in twenty years came out on Darla with LTM. A November East Coast run produced the free live CD Atlantic Crossing.
years.xp: The Powder Blind Dream followed in 2004, also produced by Massey. In May 2003 they shared a bill at London's ICA with the reunited [[Biting Tongues|555ac13e-6428-4a1a-8284-5c18d4e29330]].

years.cap: Crispy Ambulance at Sub Space, Manchester, December 2007
years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: A Factory Night (Once Again) sells out Plan K, Brussels
years.p: With Section 25, [[The Names|8bbbbdb3-544d-447a-b22c-327550e157b3]] and Kevin Hewick. LTM put it out on DVD.

eras.title: Instrumentals from the cellar
eras.text: A second reunion turned into a new direction: Hempsall moved to keyboards and the band stopped singing.

years.cap: Crispy Ambulance at the Ruby Lounge, Manchester, April 2014
years.src: The Guardian: A Factory Night · Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Record Store Day in Manchester with Section 25 and Minny Pops
years.p: The original four were back for four British dates, and the Guardian's Dave Simpson praised the reformed band's driven intensity. Leeds, Bury and London followed.

years.cap: Gary Madeley drumming on new material at SSR, Ardwick
years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Compulsion, 500 copies for Record Store Day
years.p: FBN 54, produced by Massey, includes Rain Without Clouds, held back from the Plateau Phase sessions since 1981.

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: The Subliminal Impulse Review at the Dulcimer, Chorlton
years.p: The first of four multimedia nights, with Hempsall now on keyboards and synths.
years.xp: Hempsall: "It didn't seem rewarding to keep doing our back catalogue just for the sake of it."

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Random Textures, an all-instrumental double CD
years.p: Factory Benelux paired it with an expanded Compulsion.
years.xp: Hempsall's description: "the sound of us spooking ourselves in our cellar studio".

years.src: Factory Benelux: Crispy Ambulance · LTM: Crispy Ambulance
years.h: Stratos surfaces; Reset:Decoder stays unfinished
years.p: The track appeared on Factory Benelux's Constellation de Comportements. Hempsall went on as half of Scissorgun; Madeley, Davenport and Darbyshire play as DNR.
